text: Not everything can be instrumented the way Northbridge's checkout service was in the last lesson. You don't control the source code of the Linux kernel or Kubernetes itself. That's what exporters are for — and since checkout runs on Kubernetes, this lesson also covers how Prometheus discovers a cluster that's constantly changing shape underneath it.

An exporter is a small HTTP server that translates a system's native metrics into Prometheus's text exposition format. Node exporter is the one nearly every team runs — here it is starting up, listing its enabled collectors for CPU, memory, disk, and network, before it starts listening on port 9100 for Prometheus to scrape.

Kubernetes service discovery produces a set of discovered labels for every pod it finds — things like its IP address and namespace — and relabeling rules decide what happens next: keep or drop the target, and which labels survive, possibly renamed. This is exactly how Northbridge scrapes only checkout's pods instead of the entire cluster: one relabeling rule keeps only pods carrying a scrape annotation.

Node exporter only sees the machine. It has no idea whether a Kubernetes Deployment has the right number of replicas, or whether a pod is stuck pending and never scheduled. That's kube-state-metrics — it watches the Kubernetes API and exposes the state of Kubernetes objects themselves, the other half of "is the cluster healthy," separate entirely from whether the application code running on it is healthy.

Machine health, cluster state, and application metrics — three distinct layers, all scraped the exact same way through the pull model introduced back in lesson fourteen. Next up, lesson eighteen: turning all of these PromQL queries into real Grafana dashboards.
